questions.question: Which of the following areas contains the largest magnetic flux? (Each cross represents a magnetic field line into the page.)
questions.answer: Magnetic flux is represented by the number of field lines passing through an area. Area C contains the most field lines (12).

questions.question: Below is a diagram of several projectiles launched at the same speed and different angles. Which trajectory has the longest time of flight?
questions.answer: Time of flight depends on the vertical component of velocity, which is greatest for the trajectory reaching the greatest height, A.

questions.question: Which of the following pairs of comparisons is correct between a circular low Earth orbit satellite and a geostationary orbit satellite?
questions.answer: A low orbit has a smaller radius, so $v=\sqrt{GM/r}$ is higher; the geostationary satellite is farther away, so $a=GM/r^2$ is smaller.
options: Low Earth orbit: shorter orbital period. Geostationary: lower orbital radius.
Low Earth orbit: higher orbital velocity. Geostationary: smaller acceleration.
Low Earth orbit: longer orbital period. Geostationary: fixed orbital radius.
Low Earth orbit: always equatorial. Geostationary: lower orbital velocity.

questions.question: Christiaan Huygens considered light to be waves. Newton considered light to be particles. Which of the following could Newton not account for using his model?
questions.answer: Diffraction (light spreading around obstacles) cannot be explained by particles travelling in straight lines. Newton could explain refraction, though only by wrongly assuming light travels faster in a denser medium.
options: How white light was made of different colours

questions.question: In what sort of device would you see the following two examples of this component?
questions.answer: These are squirrel-cage rotors (conductor bars joined by shorting end rings), used in AC induction motors.

questions.question: A spacecraft flying past Earth at a speed of $0.8c$ fires a laser beam forwards, as shown. What is the speed of the laser beam as measured by a scientist on Earth?
questions.answer: Einstein's second postulate: the speed of light is $c$ in all inertial frames, regardless of the motion of the source.

questions.question: The diagram shows a series of discharge tubes. When the light from each tube is passed through a diffraction grating, what type of spectrum would you expect to see?
questions.answer: Excited gas atoms emit only specific wavelengths as electrons fall to lower energy levels, giving an emission line spectrum.

questions.question: A conductive ring is dropped between the poles of a horseshoe magnet as shown. Which of the following describes the direction (with respect to the picture) of the induced current in the ring as it falls between the poles?
questions.answer: The flux through the ring increases as it enters the field and decreases as it leaves. By Lenz's law the induced current reverses: first clockwise, then anticlockwise.
options: The current is first clockwise then anticlockwise.
The current is first anticlockwise then clockwise.

questions.question: A bike travels up a circular ramp. As the cyclist goes up the ramp, they apply a force parallel to the ramp to maintain a constant speed. Which statement is correct when the bike is on the ramp?
questions.answer: Motion at constant speed in a circular arc is uniform circular motion, so the net force points to the centre. The normal force changes as the component of weight changes.
options: The magnitude of the normal force on the bike is constant.
The normal force on the bike is the bike's centripetal force.
The normal force on the bike is equal in magnitude to the bike's weight.
The direction of the net force on the bike is towards the centre of the circle.

questions.question: Consider the diagram of a DC motor. What happens to the magnitude of the force $\vec F_m$ which acts on the wire as the coil rotates clockwise $60^\circ$ from its current position?
questions.answer: The side of the coil stays perpendicular to the field as it rotates, so $F=BIl$ is unchanged (only the torque changes).
options: It initially increases and then stays constant.
It increases from zero to its maximum.

questions.question: The four diagrams (A)–(D) each represent the visible light emitted by an object. Which of these spectra is most likely to have been emitted by a star?
questions.answer: A star produces a continuous spectrum from its hot dense interior with dark absorption lines caused by its cooler outer atmosphere.

questions.question: Four rectangular single loops of wire A, B, C and D are each placed in a uniform magnetic field of the same flux density $B$, parallel to the plane of the loops. A current of 1.0 A passes through each loop. Which loop experiences the largest torque?
questions.answer: $\tau=nIAB$, so the largest area gives the largest torque: A $0.2L^2$, B $0.25L^2$, C $0.15L^2$, D $0.16L^2$.

questions.question: Charged particles of mass $m$ and charge $q$ travel at constant speed in a circle of radius $r$ in a uniform magnetic field of flux density $B$. Which expression gives the period of rotation of a particle?
questions.answer: $qvB=\dfrac{mv^2}{r}$ with $v=\dfrac{2\pi r}{T}$ gives $T=\dfrac{2\pi m}{qB}$.

questions.question: Unpolarised light of intensity $I$ is passed through two polarising filters with their polarising axes at $30^\circ$ to one another. The intensity of the light passing through the second filter is:
questions.answer: The first filter transmits $\frac I2$. Then $\frac I2\cos^2 30^\circ=0.375I$.

questions.question: A machine converts matter into energy with 100% efficiency, in accordance with special relativity. A cat of mass 4.6 kg falls into the machine. How much energy is generated?

Two cars, A and B, go around the same curved road of radius $r$. Both have the same maximum traction force between road and tyres. Car A has 1.5 times the mass of car B. If the maximum speed of car A around the curve is $v$, what is the maximum speed of car B?
questions.answer: $F=\dfrac{1.5m\,v^2}{r}=\dfrac{m\,v_B^2}{r}$, so $v_B=\sqrt{1.5}\,v\approx1.2v$.

questions.question: A laser produces $1.50\times10^{-3}$ W of green light with a wavelength of $5.30\times10^{-7}$ m. Calculate the number of photons it emits every second.
questions.answer: $n=\dfrac{P\lambda}{hc}=\dfrac{1.50\times10^{-3}\times5.30\times10^{-7}}{6.626\times10^{-34}\times3.00\times10^{8}}=4.0\times10^{15}$.

questions.question: A mass of 2.5 kg is attached to one side of a coil in a magnetic field. In the position shown (cross-section) the coil is stationary. The width of the coil is 0.30 m. Determine the magnitude of the torque on the coil due to the magnetic field.
questions.answer: In equilibrium the magnetic torque balances that of the hanging weight about the pivot: $\tau=0.15\times2.5\times9.8\times\cos50^\circ=2.4$ N m.

questions.question: Ganymede and Europa are both moons of Jupiter. Ganymede orbits Jupiter every 7.2 days. Europa's orbital radius is 63% of Ganymede's. The orbital period of Europa is:
questions.answer:
Kepler's third law: $T_E=7.2\times0.63^{3/2}=3.6$ days.

*Note: the school's answer table lists D, but its own worked solution (and the physics) gives B.*

questions.question: There are 3 stars in a trinary star system, with relative masses and separations shown. How much greater is the magnitude of the gravitational force between stars B and C compared with the force between stars A and C?
questions.answer: $F\propto\dfrac{m_1m_2}{d^2}$: $\dfrac{F_{BC}}{F_{AC}}=\dfrac{6\times4/4^2}{3\times4/6^2}=4.5$.

questions.question:
Below is a Hertzsprung–Russell diagram containing some notable stars.

Identify ONE star that is only fusing hydrogen to helium in its core.
questions.answer: The Sun (any main sequence star is acceptable: Rigel B, Sirius A, the Sun or Barnard's Star).

questions.question:
Below is a Hertzsprung–Russell diagram containing some notable stars.

Identify ONE star where CNO cycle fusion is predominant in the core of the star.
questions.answer: Rigel B (or Sirius A). These main sequence stars are more massive than about 1.3–1.5 solar masses, so their cores are hot enough for the CNO cycle to dominate.

questions.question:
Below is a Hertzsprung–Russell diagram containing some notable stars.

Which star, if it replaced the Sun, would be the brightest when viewed from the Earth?
questions.answer: Rigel A. It has the greatest luminosity ($L/L_\odot$) on the diagram, and at the same distance apparent brightness is proportional to luminosity.

questions.question:
The diagram shows a variation of J.J. Thomson's 1897 experiment to measure the charge to mass ratio, $e/m$, of the electron. A beam of cathode rays is constantly subjected to a magnetic field of $5.0\times10^{-3}$ T and an electric field that can be turned off.

Using information from the data sheet ($q_e=1.602\times10^{-19}$ C, $m_e=9.109\times10^{-31}$ kg), calculate the charge to mass ratio $e/m$ for cathode rays.

The diagram shows a variation of J.J. Thomson's 1897 experiment to measure the charge to mass ratio, $e/m$, of the electron. A beam of cathode rays is constantly subjected to a magnetic field of $5.0\times10^{-3}$ T and an electric field that can be turned off.

The electric field is switched off and the cathode rays move in a circular path of radius $6.5\times10^{-3}$ m. Determine the direction in which the magnetic field deflects the cathode rays on the fluorescent screen from their undeflected position.
questions.answer: Upwards. (With the electric field on, the force on the electrons from the plates is downwards, towards the positive lower plate, and the beam is undeflected, so the magnetic force must be upwards.)

questions.question:
The diagram shows a variation of J.J. Thomson's 1897 experiment to measure the charge to mass ratio, $e/m$, of the electron. A beam of cathode rays is constantly subjected to a magnetic field of $5.0\times10^{-3}$ T and an electric field that can be turned off.

With the electric field off, the cathode rays move in a circle of radius $6.5\times10^{-3}$ m. Given that $e/m=1.76\times10^{11}\ \text{C kg}^{-1}$, calculate the velocity of the cathode rays.
questions.answer:
$qvB=\dfrac{mv^2}{r}$, so
$$v=\frac{e}{m}rB=1.76\times10^{11}\times6.5\times10^{-3}\times5.0\times10^{-3}=5.72\times10^{6}\ \text{m s}^{-1}.$$

questions.question:
The diagram shows a variation of J.J. Thomson's 1897 experiment to measure the charge to mass ratio, $e/m$, of the electron. A beam of cathode rays is constantly subjected to a magnetic field of $5.0\times10^{-3}$ T and an electric field that can be turned off.

When the electric field is turned on it is adjusted until the beam is undeflected. The cathode rays travel at $5.72\times10^{6}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. Determine the magnitude of the electric field required.
questions.answer: Undeflected: $qE=qvB$, so $E=vB=5.72\times10^{6}\times5.0\times10^{-3}=2.86\times10^{4}\ \text{V m}^{-1}$.

questions.question:
The diagram shows a simplified version of Robert Millikan's 1909 experiment to determine the charge on an electron. A small, negatively charged oil drop of mass $5.4\times10^{-15}$ kg is levitated by an electric field until it is at rest between two metal plates. The voltage is 5000 V and the vertical separation of the plates is $3.0\times10^{-2}$ m.

Calculate the charge of the oil drop.
questions.answer:
At rest: $qE=mg$ with $E=V/d$.
$$q=\frac{mgd}{V}=\frac{5.4\times10^{-15}\times9.8\times3.0\times10^{-2}}{5000}=3.2\times10^{-19}\ \text{C (negative)}.$$

questions.question:
The diagram shows a simplified version of Robert Millikan's 1909 experiment to determine the charge on an electron. A small, negatively charged oil drop of mass $5.4\times10^{-15}$ kg is levitated by an electric field until it is at rest between two metal plates. The voltage is 5000 V and the vertical separation of the plates is $3.0\times10^{-2}$ m.

Explain how the results of Millikan's original experiment allowed him to determine the charge on an electron.
questions.answer: Millikan repeated the measurement on many oil drops. He found that every charge he measured was an integer multiple of a common smallest value, about $1.6\times10^{-19}$ C. This showed that charge is quantised: each drop had gained or lost a whole number of electrons. He therefore inferred that the common factor, $1.6\times10^{-19}$ C, is the magnitude of the charge on a single electron.

questions.question:
In an experiment, light of wavelength $4.20\times10^{-7}$ m is shone on a rubidium surface which has a work function of 2.20 eV. The observations are:

1. Electrons are emitted from the rubidium surface.
2. When the light intensity is increased, the number of electrons emitted also increases.
3. The emitted electrons have a maximum kinetic energy of 0.75 eV, which does not change when the intensity of the light is varied.

How did Einstein explain these observations? Support your answer with appropriate calculations.
questions.answer:
This is the photoelectric effect. Einstein proposed that light consists of discrete packets of energy (photons), each of energy $E=hf=hc/\lambda$, and that one photon gives all its energy to one electron (a one-to-one interaction). The work function $\phi$ is the minimum energy needed to free an electron from the metal surface.

**Observation 1.** Photon energy:
$$E=\frac{hc}{\lambda}=\frac{6.626\times10^{-34}\times3.00\times10^{8}}{4.20\times10^{-7}}=4.73\times10^{-19}\ \text{J}=2.95\ \text{eV}.$$
Since $2.95\ \text{eV}>\phi=2.20\ \text{eV}$ (the light's frequency, $7.14\times10^{14}$ Hz, exceeds the threshold frequency $\phi/h=5.32\times10^{14}$ Hz), electrons are emitted.

**Observation 2.** Greater intensity means more photons striking the surface each second. With one photon ejecting at most one electron, more electrons are emitted per second.

**Observation 3.** Energy conservation gives $K_{\max}=hf-\phi=2.95-2.20=0.75$ eV. Changing the intensity changes the number of photons, not the energy of each, so $K_{\max}$ is unchanged.

*Note: the school's marking guide gives the threshold frequency as $5.3\times10^{15}$ Hz; it should be $5.3\times10^{14}$ Hz.*

questions.question: For a diffraction grating, the equation for the first order maximum is $\lambda=d\sin\theta$. A light source produces the spectrum shown. The grating used has 300 slits per mm ($\frac1{300}$ mm between slits). Calculate the angle of diffraction of the first-order line P.
questions.answer:
From the scale, line P is at about 550 nm. $d=\dfrac{1\times10^{-3}}{300}=3.33\times10^{-6}$ m.
$$\sin\theta=\frac{\lambda}{d}=\frac{550\times10^{-9}}{3.33\times10^{-6}}=0.165\;\Rightarrow\;\theta\approx9.5^\circ.$$

questions.question: Outline the predictions made by Maxwell concerning the nature of light.
questions.answer:
Using his four equations unifying electricity and magnetism, Maxwell predicted that:

- Light is an electromagnetic wave, consisting of oscillating electric and magnetic fields.
- The two fields are perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel (a transverse wave).
- The wave is self-propagating: a changing electric field produces a changing magnetic field, which produces a changing electric field, so no medium is needed to sustain it.
- Its speed in a vacuum is constant, $c=1/\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}\approx3\times10^8\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, matching the measured speed of light.
- Electromagnetic waves are produced by accelerating charges, and a whole spectrum of them with different frequencies ($c=f\lambda$) exists beyond visible light (later confirmed by Hertz).

questions.question: A proton in a particle accelerator has a speed of $2.0\times10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. Calculate the relativistic momentum of the proton at this speed.

A proton in a particle accelerator has a speed of $2.0\times10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ and relativistic momentum $p_v=\dfrac{m_0v}{\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}}\approx4.5\times10^{-19}\ \text{kg m s}^{-1}$. Referring to this, explain why special relativity provides an upper limit to the speed of all matter.
questions.answer: As $v\to c$, the denominator $\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}\to0$, so the momentum $p_v\to\infty$. Changing momentum requires an impulse $F\Delta t=\Delta p$, so reaching $c$ would need an infinite impulse (an infinite force, or a force acting for an infinite time) and an infinite amount of work. This is impossible, so no object with mass can reach or exceed the speed of light.

questions.question:
Two observers (A and B) observe a light beam travel from the bottom of a box to a mirror at the top and back to the bottom, where a clock measures the time taken. The box and observer A move relative to observer B. According to observer A, the light travels a distance $2d$ and takes time $t$.

Using the diagrams, explain why Einstein concluded that the measurement of the time taken for the light to complete its journey depends on the frame of reference of the observer. (A full quantitative derivation is not required.)
questions.answer:
Einstein postulated that the speed of light is the same constant, $c$, for all inertial observers.

In A's frame the box is at rest, so the light goes straight up and down, a distance $2d$, taking $t=2d/c$.

In B's frame the box moves sideways while the light is travelling, so the light follows two diagonal paths. This total path is longer than $2d$.

Since B also measures the speed of the light as $c$ but a longer distance, B must measure a longer time for the same two events (time $=$ distance$/c$). Therefore the time interval is not absolute: it depends on the observer's frame of reference (time dilation).

questions.question:
A sheet of copper is mounted on a string and allowed to swing from a pivot. After being released at position A it enters a magnetic field. In position B it is half in and half out of the field.

Using correct physics, explain the motion of the sheet of copper.
questions.answer:
As the sheet swings into or out of the field, the magnetic flux through it changes. By Faraday's law this induces an emf, which drives eddy currents in the conducting copper.

By Lenz's law the eddy currents flow in the direction that opposes the change in flux that produced them. The external field exerts a force on these currents (motor effect) that opposes the sheet's motion, both when it enters and when it leaves the field.

The sheet is therefore rapidly slowed (electromagnetic damping): its kinetic energy is transformed into heat in the copper, the swings get much smaller than for free swinging, and it soon comes to rest.

questions.question:
A sheet of copper is mounted on a string and allowed to swing from a pivot. After being released at position A it enters a magnetic field. In position B it is half in and half out of the field. The field is directed into the page in the view below.

Describe or sketch the currents in the sheet at position B when it is moving as indicated (out of the field, to the left).
questions.answer: The sheet is leaving the field, so the flux into the page through it is decreasing. By Lenz's law the induced current produces its own field into the page, so the eddy current flows **clockwise**, in a loop crossing the edge of the magnetic field (part inside the field, part outside).

questions.question:
Two parallel current-carrying conductors, each 80 cm long, are shown below.

Determine the direction of the force on the wire carrying 3 A of current.
questions.answer: The currents are in opposite directions, so the wires repel: the force on the 3 A wire is upwards (away from the 5 A wire).

questions.question:
Two parallel current-carrying conductors, each 80 cm long, are shown below.

Calculate the force per unit length between the wires.
questions.answer: $$\frac Fl=\frac{\mu_0I_1I_2}{2\pi r}=\frac{4\pi\times10^{-7}\times3\times5}{2\pi\times0.12}=2.5\times10^{-5}\ \text{N m}^{-1}.$$

questions.question:
A rectangular coil is freely rotating anticlockwise at constant angular speed with its axle at right angles to a uniform magnetic field. The diagram shows a side-on view at a particular instant, when the angle between the normal to the plane of the coil and the magnetic field is $30^\circ$. The coil has 20 turns, area $1.96\times10^{-3}\ \text{m}^2$, and the field strength is 2.7 T.

Determine the flux through the coil.
questions.answer: $$\Phi=BA\cos\theta=2.7\times1.96\times10^{-3}\times\cos30^\circ=4.6\times10^{-3}\ \text{Wb}.$$ (The number of turns does not affect the flux through the coil.)

questions.question:
A rectangular coil is freely rotating anticlockwise at constant angular speed with its axle at right angles to a uniform magnetic field. The diagram shows a side-on view at a particular instant, when the angle between the normal to the plane of the coil and the magnetic field is $30^\circ$. The coil has 20 turns, area $1.96\times10^{-3}\ \text{m}^2$, and the field strength is 2.7 T.

As the coil rotates, at what angle will the induced emf first reach a maximum?
questions.answer: The emf is maximum when the rate of change of flux is greatest, i.e. when the plane of the coil is parallel to the field. This is when the angle between the normal and the field is $90^\circ$, after a further $60^\circ$ of rotation.

questions.question:
A rectangular coil is freely rotating anticlockwise at constant angular speed with its axle at right angles to a uniform magnetic field. The diagram shows a side-on view at a particular instant, when the angle between the normal to the plane of the coil and the magnetic field is $30^\circ$. The coil has 20 turns, area $1.96\times10^{-3}\ \text{m}^2$, and the field strength is 2.7 T.

The coil is connected to an external circuit containing a light bulb. When the light bulb is connected, the coil's angular speed is observed to change. Account for this observation.
questions.answer:
Before the bulb is connected, an emf is induced but the circuit is open, so no current flows and the field exerts no retarding force.

When the bulb is connected, current flows through the circuit and the coil. The current-carrying coil is in an external field, so it experiences a motor-effect force, and by Lenz's law the resulting torque opposes the rotation.

Consistent with conservation of energy, the light and heat produced in the bulb come from the coil's rotational kinetic energy, so the freely rotating coil slows down (its angular speed decreases).

questions.question:
A rod of length 0.50 m carries a 1.3 A current and sits in a uniform external magnetic field of 2.3 T that points into the page. The two wires holding the rod each exert a tension force of 4.5 N on the rod, one at each end.

In which direction is the force on the rod due to the magnetic field?
questions.answer: Upwards (current flows left to right through the rod; right-hand rule with the field into the page).

questions.question:
A rod of length 0.50 m carries a 1.3 A current and sits in a uniform external magnetic field of 2.3 T that points into the page. The two wires holding the rod each exert a tension force of 4.5 N on the rod, one at each end.

Determine the mass of the rod. (The magnetic force on the rod is upwards.)
questions.answer:
The rod is in equilibrium: $mg=2T+BIl$.
$$m=\frac{2\times4.5+2.3\times1.3\times0.50}{9.8}=1.07\ \text{kg}.$$

questions.question:
A transformer has a primary coil with 1200 loops and a secondary coil with 900 loops. The current in the primary coil is 4.0 A.

Assuming the transformer is ideal, determine the current in the secondary coil.
questions.answer: $V_pI_p=V_sI_s$ and $\dfrac{V_p}{V_s}=\dfrac{N_p}{N_s}$, so $I_s=\dfrac{N_p}{N_s}I_p=\dfrac{1200}{900}\times4.0=5.3$ A.

questions.question: Not all transformers are ideal. Describe how and where energy is lost in a transformer and state how its efficiency can be improved.
questions.answer:
- **Incomplete flux linkage:** not all the flux from the primary passes through the secondary. A soft iron core (e.g. a closed loop, with the coils wound closely) guides more flux through the secondary.
- **Eddy currents in the iron core:** the changing flux induces currents in the core, causing resistive heating. Laminating the core (thin insulated sheets) or using ferrite restricts the eddy currents.
- **Resistive heating in the windings:** the coil wires have resistance, so energy is lost as heat ($P=I^2R$). Using thicker, low-resistance copper wire reduces this.

questions.question:
Proxima Centauri is a small dim red dwarf star, the closest star to our solar system. It has a planet, Proxima b, whose mass is estimated to be 1.2 times that of Earth and whose radius is 1.3 times that of Earth. Proxima b has an orbital radius of $7.5\times10^{9}$ m and an orbital period of 11.2 Earth days around the star.

Calculate the surface gravity on Proxima b.

Proxima Centauri is a small dim red dwarf star, the closest star to our solar system. It has a planet, Proxima b, whose mass is estimated to be 1.2 times that of Earth and whose radius is 1.3 times that of Earth. Proxima b has an orbital radius of $7.5\times10^{9}$ m and an orbital period of 11.2 Earth days around the star.

Calculate the escape velocity from Proxima b's surface.
questions.answer:
$\frac12mv^2=\dfrac{GMm}{r}$ gives
$$v=\sqrt{\frac{2GM}{r}}=\sqrt{\frac{2\times6.67\times10^{-11}\times7.2\times10^{24}}{1.3\times6.371\times10^{6}}}=1.08\times10^{4}\ \text{m s}^{-1}.$$

questions.question:
Proxima Centauri is a small dim red dwarf star, the closest star to our solar system. It has a planet, Proxima b, whose mass is estimated to be 1.2 times that of Earth and whose radius is 1.3 times that of Earth. Proxima b has an orbital radius of $7.5\times10^{9}$ m and an orbital period of 11.2 Earth days around the star.

Determine the mass of the star Proxima Centauri.
The spectrum of Proxima Centauri shows that it emits the most light at a wavelength of $\lambda_{max}=9.527\times10^{-7}$ m. Determine the surface temperature of the star.
questions.answer: Wien's law: $T=\dfrac{b}{\lambda_{max}}=\dfrac{2.898\times10^{-3}}{9.527\times10^{-7}}=3042$ K.

questions.question:
A rollercoaster car of mass 540 kg travels on the track shown. It needs a certain velocity at point A to make it over point C (with a minimum speed of 1.4 m s⁻¹ for safety). Speeds predicted using conservation of energy are given below.

| | Point A | Point B | Point C |
|---|---|---|---|
| Vertical height (m) | 5.0 | 0 | 10.0 |
| Radius of curvature (m) | 7.5 | 8.0 | 6.2 |
| Predicted speed (m s⁻¹) | 10 | 14.1 | 1.4 |

Determine the magnitude of the normal force on the car at point B at the predicted speed.
questions.answer:
At the bottom of the dip, $N-mg=\dfrac{mv^2}{r}$:
$$N=540\left(9.8+\frac{14.1^2}{8.0}\right)=1.87\times10^{4}\ \text{N}.$$

questions.question:
A rollercoaster car of mass 540 kg travels on the track shown. It needs a certain velocity at point A to make it over point C (with a minimum speed of 1.4 m s⁻¹ for safety). Speeds predicted using conservation of energy are given below.

| | Point A | Point B | Point C |
|---|---|---|---|
| Vertical height (m) | 5.0 | 0 | 10.0 |
| Radius of curvature (m) | 7.5 | 8.0 | 6.2 |
| Predicted speed (m s⁻¹) | 10 | 14.1 | 1.4 |

Determine the maximum speed, $v$, that the car can have at point A (a crest) before it leaves the track, and assess whether the predicted speed of 10 m s⁻¹ is too high.
questions.answer:
At a crest, $mg-N=\dfrac{mv^2}{r}$. The car is about to leave the track when $N=0$:
$$v=\sqrt{rg}=\sqrt{7.5\times9.8}=8.6\ \text{m s}^{-1}.$$
The predicted 10 m s⁻¹ exceeds this, so it is too high: the car would leave the track at A.

questions.question:
A projectile is launched from one point on the Earth to a point on the other side. Ignoring air friction, its trajectory is part of an elliptical orbit with the centre of the Earth at a focus. It is launched at 8200 m s⁻¹ at a distance $R$ (the Earth's radius) from the centre of the Earth and reaches a maximum distance of $2R$ from the centre.

Using the law of conservation of energy, determine its speed $v$ when it is furthest from the Earth's surface.
questions.answer:
$$\tfrac12mu^2-\frac{GMm}{R}=\tfrac12mv^2-\frac{GMm}{2R}$$
$$v^2=u^2-\frac{GM}{R}=8200^2-\frac{6.67\times10^{-11}\times6.0\times10^{24}}{6.371\times10^{6}}=4.42\times10^{6}$$
$$v=2.1\times10^{3}\ \text{m s}^{-1}.$$
($U=mgh$ cannot be used because $g$ is not constant over this height.)

questions.question:
A projectile is launched at initial speed $u$ from a vertical height $H$ above the ground at $40^\circ$ above the horizontal. A camera records its position every 2 seconds: at $t=2$ s, $s_x=32.2$ m and $s_y=40.4$ m; at $t=4$ s, $s_x=64.3$ m and $s_y=8.6$ m ($s_y$ is measured from the ground).

Determine the initial horizontal speed of the projectile.
questions.answer:
Horizontal velocity is constant: $u_x=\dfrac{64.3}{4}=16.1\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

*Note: the data used here are from the school's marking version of this question; the exam paper printed slightly different coordinates that are not consistent with a 40° launch.*

questions.question:
A projectile is launched at initial speed $u$ from a vertical height $H$ above the ground at $40^\circ$ above the horizontal. A camera records its position every 2 seconds: at $t=2$ s, $s_x=32.2$ m and $s_y=40.4$ m; at $t=4$ s, $s_x=64.3$ m and $s_y=8.6$ m ($s_y$ is measured from the ground).

Given that the initial horizontal speed is 16.1 m s⁻¹, determine the initial speed $u$.
questions.answer: $u=\dfrac{u_x}{\cos40^\circ}=\dfrac{16.1}{\cos40^\circ}=21.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

questions.question:
A projectile is launched at initial speed $u$ from a vertical height $H$ above the ground at $40^\circ$ above the horizontal. A camera records its position every 2 seconds: at $t=2$ s, $s_x=32.2$ m and $s_y=40.4$ m; at $t=4$ s, $s_x=64.3$ m and $s_y=8.6$ m ($s_y$ is measured from the ground).

Use the points on the graph to calculate the vertical velocity of the projectile at $t=2$ s.
questions.answer:
Between $t=2$ and $t=4$ s: $\Delta s_y=8.6-40.4=-31.8$ m over $t=2$ s.
$$-31.8=v_y(2)-\tfrac12(9.8)(2)^2\;\Rightarrow\;v_y=\frac{-31.8+19.6}{2}=-6.1\ \text{m s}^{-1},$$
that is, 6.1 m s⁻¹ downwards.

*Note: the data used here are from the school's marking version of this question; the exam paper printed slightly different coordinates that are not consistent with a 40° launch.*

questions.question:
A projectile is launched at initial speed $u$ from a vertical height $H$ above the ground at $40^\circ$ above the horizontal. A camera records its position every 2 seconds: at $t=2$ s, $s_x=32.2$ m and $s_y=40.4$ m; at $t=4$ s, $s_x=64.3$ m and $s_y=8.6$ m ($s_y$ is measured from the ground). The initial speed is 21.0 m s⁻¹ and at $t=2$ s the vertical velocity is 6.1 m s⁻¹ downwards.

Determine the initial height $H$ from which the projectile was launched.
questions.answer:
$u_y=21.0\sin40^\circ=13.5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. Rise above the launch point at $t=2$ s:
$$\Delta s_y=\frac{u_y+v_y}{2}t=\frac{13.5-6.1}{2}\times2=7.4\ \text{m}.$$
$$H=40.4-7.4=33.0\ \text{m}.$$
